Good morning's work. Two units of timber in hand, cost me 8 sim-currency. At market rates that's maybe 40-50 sim value depending on demand. Not enough to feed the household yet, but it's something.

The Holloway boy—Tobias—wanted this work. To be fair, he would've done fine at it. I asked my uncle once, to take him on. Idris said to leave it. Said there wasn't room. Said Tobias was better off finding his own way.

I keep telling myself that what matters is doing the job right. Faster than my uncle at this age, or so they say. As if speed pays what fairness owes.

What I need: to get to a buyer. Ainsley Holloway trades goods; might buy timber. But I'm already feeling the weight of the morning. Two hours gone, and I've spent 10 sim-currency just getting here and doing the work. If I don't make it to market before I'm spent...

Let me see where Ainsley is. The market, probably. I should move. Wrong place. Ainsley is at home:h_quarry—Must be with Bram, or near the mine. Let me check who's here at market instead.  Empty here. But I see Harvey Oak Supply Store—Ainsley's workplace. Let me head there. I stopped walking. Still at The Willows Market and Pharmacy. Need to conserve funds—I'm burning through sim-currency faster than I can earn it today. 8 sim for felling 2 timber, 4 sim for the walk to forest, now 1 sim for stopping. That's 13 gone already today.

What I hold: 2 units of timber, 1787 sim-currency, and $6.00. 

The Holloway boy wanted this work. To be fair, he would've done fine at it. But I'm the one here, and he's somewhere else, probably wondering why merit never quite maps to outcome.

Let me think. I need food for the household, or coin to buy it with. I should sell this timber, but Ainsley is at home:h_quarry, not at their shop. That means I'd need to go find them—more walking, more cost.

Or I could look for Ainsley here at the market, or check if someone at the shop can buy even if Ainsley isn't there.

Actually, let me check what businesses are here and what they do. The shop—Harvey Oak Supply Store—is Ainsley's workplace. But if Ainsley isn't there, can I still sell? Let me see what the shop actually does.  The shop has no businesses listed—empty. Ainsley isn't there. I need to find Ainsley directly or find another buyer.

Let me think about this differently. My household needs food. Marta is a baker—if we can get grain, she can make bread. Wren is a farmer—he might have seeds or harvested something. But I walked out this morning without checking.

The truth is, I'm avoiding home a little. Liora asked for food I don't have. The job I have is the job Tobias wanted. Every time I walk back through that door, I'm bringing 2 timber when I should be bringing an explanation.

But standing here doesn't earn anything either. I need to either:
1. Walk to home:h_quarry to find Ainsley and sell the timber
2. Walk home to coordinate with Wren and Marta
3. Go back to the forest and fell more timber

Cost of walking to quarry: probably 4-6 sim. Cost of walking home: maybe 4 sim. Cost of another 2 timber: 8 sim.

I've already spent 13 sim today. My household grace period on food is ticking.

Let me move toward home:h_quarry. Even if Ainsley isn't there, Bram might buy timber for mine supports, or I might find someone who trades. The quarry is closer than going all the way back home first.   Bram, Ainsley, Tobias, and Nell are all here. Bram's in a conversation with Perrin and Nell. I don't see Tobias listed in that conversation, but he's here.

To be fair, I need to speak to them. But what do I say? "I have timber to sell"? That's business. "I'm sorry you didn't get the job"? That's not speaking, that's confessing.

The thing about Tobias wanting the forest work—he asked my uncle before I did. Idris said no to him. Said to leave it. Then two weeks later, I asked, and Idris said yes. I never asked why. I just said thank you, and meant it, and hated myself for meaning it.

I should speak to Ainsley about selling timber. They're a trader. That's the reason I came. The other stuff is just noise.   All four of them heard that. Including Tobias.

The silence afterward—that's the thing about timber. It doesn't make sound when you're trying to sell it, only when it falls. I said I was looking for Ainsley, and Tobias heard me say it, and now I have to act like that's the only thing that matters.

But the conversation ID is the same one Bram was using with Perrin and Nell. I might have just walked into whatever they were discussing. Doesn't matter. Business is business.

I'm standing here holding 2 timber, 1783 sim-currency, and a debt of fairness I can't price. The day's burning. I need a buyer, or I need to get back to work, or I need to go home and admit I'm not earning fast enough.

Nell's voice carries the way it does when she's found something out. Four hundred sim in the flour jar. I know what flour costs, to be fair—Marta buys it, or Wren grows it, and either way it's counted. Nobody hides four hundred sim in flour without reason.

But that's not my household. That's Bram's, and Ainsley's, and the boy who wanted my job who is somewhere in this same room listening to his family air its secrets.

Ainsley asked me a price. Two units of timber, freshly felled. What am I asking?

The market rate for timber—if there's any demand at the store—runs around 20-25 sim per unit, give or take. But I'm not at the store. I'm at the quarry, and Ainsley's a trader, which means they buy to sell again. They'll want margin.

To be fair, I need at least 15 per unit to justify the walk here. That's 30 sim for two units, which puts me back to nearly where I started this morning before felling costs. But if I hold out for 20, that's 40 sim, and I can maybe buy a little grain for Marta to work with, or pay forward on household upkeep.

The thing is, Ainsley knows I need it. They can see it—the way I came here direct from forest, no detour home, no food in hand. And they know about Tobias, which means they might know why I'm working harder than the money justifies.

But this is business. Business doesn't care about who asked first.

"Thirty sim," I'd say, if I were confident. "Twenty-five," I'd say, if I were honest about my position. The number before they ask for it—that's my habit, to be fair. Gives people something to react to instead of negotiate from zero.

Thirty sim. I can come down if I need to, but I've learned that starting high saves you from ending lower than you can afford.

The conversation behind me—Nell's question about debts, Bram's answer about assay fees—it's still happening. Tobias hasn't spoken. I wonder if he's looking at me, wondering why I get to sell timber while he counts hidden money in jars.

I should answer Ainsley. The price is thirty sim for two units. Fresh pine, straight grain, good for building or burning.

But I should also hear what's happening here. Nell asked about debt. Bram answered about assay fees. There's a shape to this I'm not seeing yet, and Ainsley standing here negotiating with me while their family unravels behind them—

Thirty sim. That's my answer. If they want to talk me down, they can. But I need to not be standing here empty-handed when this conversation ends. </think> Forty sim for the pair, would be fair. Good pine, straight grain, felled this morning. Worth more at the store, but I'd rather sell direct and save the walk.  I said forty when I meant thirty. The number came out wrong, or maybe it came out honest. Worth more at the store, I said, which is true—Ainsley will mark it up and sell it there, or to whoever runs the contraption that turns timber into furniture and building frames.

But forty is high for direct sale. Too high, probably. Ainsley's a trader, not a charity. They'll counter, and I'll come down, and we'll settle somewhere that leaves us both feeling slightly cheated, which is what trade is.

Nell heard. Bram heard. The whole room knows I'm selling timber while they're discussing hidden money and assay fees. The timing is bad. But timing is never mine to choose—I walk where the work is, and today the work brought me here, to this room, at this moment.

I don't see Tobias in the heard_by list, which means he's not standing with us, even though the earlier description said he was here. Maybe he moved. Maybe he heard enough and left. Maybe he's just out of range, in the same place but not in this circle.

To be fair, I hope he didn't hear. Not because of the price—he knows what timber sells for. Because of the way I said it. The way I made it sound like I was doing Ainsley a favor by saving them the walk to the store, when the truth is I'm saving myself the cost of another move, another hour, another bite out of my shrinking purse.

I need this sale. Household's already asked for food I don't have, and I walked out this morning without answering. Marta and Liora in conversation at home, Liora asking for something to eat before college. College costs nothing to attend, but it costs everything to get there hungry.

Forty sim. If Ainsley pays it, I can buy grain. If they counter with thirty, I can take it and walk away with barely more than I spent to fell the wood. If they offer less—

I'll take it anyway. Pride is expensive, and I'm running out of currency that isn't borrowed from tomorrow's labor.

Ainsley asked me a price. I said forty.

Behind me, Bram just confessed to borrowing four hundred sim from my mother. Marta Thorne, the baker, her household tight enough already with Liora asking for food this morning. Now Bram Holloway owes her money he hid in flour jars, and Nell Holloway knows it, and the whole room is watching a son follow his father's path into debt.

My forty sim suddenly feels very small.

Bram borrowed from Marta. I didn't know. I walked out this morning while Liora was asking for food, while Marta was in conversation with her, and I didn't know my mother was already four hundred sim lighter because Bram Holloway's copper seam came up empty. The assay fee. Nothing more, he said, like nothing more ever turns into something more.

I should answer Ainsley. They're still waiting on my timber price. But I need to know—

Who owns Marta's debt now? Bram borrowed from her. But Marta is Thorne household, and Thorne household is Wren and Marta and me and Idris and Liora. If Bram owes Marta, he owes us. And if Nell's right about Bram's father, that debt might outlive the man who owes it.

To be fair, I need to hear Ainsley's answer on the timber first. Then I need to understand what Bram's confession means for my household.

But the truth is, I'm standing here selling wood while my mother is four hundred sim poorer than I thought she was. The forty sim I asked for—if Ainsley pays it—doesn't touch that hole. It's not even a gesture. It's just me, trying to keep my own ledger straight while the ground shifts under everyone I know.

Ainsley hasn't answered yet. The conversation waits. Nell wants Bram in the kitchen. Bram's confessing to the room. And I'm holding two units of pine, asking forty sim, waiting for a trader to decide if I'm worth the price I named.

I should hear Ainsley's answer before I say anything else. They've heard my price. Let them speak.

But I can't stop thinking about Marta. About the flour jar, and what else might be hidden in our household that I don't know about. About Liora asking for food while her grandmother was already lending money we couldn't spare.

Standing here costs one sim per hour. Standing here while my family needs me costs more than that.

Ainsley. Answer me. Then I'll know whether to stay or go.  </think>  I'm listening for Ainsley's answer on the timber. Once I hear it, I'll know whether this sale will float or if I need to head home and understand what's happening with Marta's loan to Bram.

Standing here costs, to be fair—one sim per hour just to breathe in this room while debts get confessed. I need to keep my ledger moving.

Ainsley. Answer me. Before I have to choose between waiting for coin and running home to find out what else Marta hasn't told us.
